Each release has two steps. First, upload every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`, alongside the existing files. Then update the manifest so it points to those new names. Browsers load the manifest to find out which files to request.

The upload comes first so that every file the new manifest names already exists when a browser reads it. If we switched first, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request files that haven't finished uploading. It would get 404s and show a broken page. Uploading first means a browser sees either the complete old set or the complete new set, never a mix.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. A page opened before the release keeps requesting the old names as it lazy-loads scripts, styles, images and route chunks. If those files were deleted, those users would hit errors partway through their session. Because each version uses distinct names, old and new files can coexist without overwriting each other.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a new versioned name (for example `app.3f9c2.js`), then switch the manifest so it points at those names.

The upload comes first because the manifest switch is what makes a release live. Once a browser fetches the new manifest, it immediately requests the files it names. If those files weren't already uploaded, the browser would get 404s and render a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references already exists, so switching the manifest moves visitors from one complete release to another in a single step.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. Those pages still request the old versioned names, for example when they lazy-load a chunk or fetch an image later in the session. If we deleted the old files at release time, those users would hit missing files partway through their visit. Because every release uses new names, the old files never conflict with the new ones, so keeping them costs nothing in correctness.

A release happens in two steps. First, we upload every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2a.js` instead of `app.js`. Then we switch the manifest so it points to those new names. Each version gets its own filenames, so a release never overwrites a file that someone might still be loading.

The upload happens before the switch because the manifest is what sends browsers to the new files. If we switched it first, some browsers would read the new manifest and request files that haven't been uploaded yet, which would fail. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already exists when browsers see it. That makes the switch a single change that is safe to make.

We keep the old assets because browsers don't all move to the new manifest at the same moment. A browser that loaded the previous manifest, whether from an open tab or a cache, will keep requesting the old filenames, often to load more of the page. If we deleted those files, those pages would break partway through. Leaving the old versions in place lets every browser finish with the version it started on and pick up the new one on its next manifest fetch.
